topic: Emergencies and abnormal operations under IFR

notes.front: What is partial panel flight?
notes.back: Flying by instruments with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative.
notes.explanation: The handbook says every manoeuvre except the instrument takeoff can be flown this way.
notes.example: Like driving at night with the speedometer and sat-nav dark, but steering by the gauges that still work.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 7, Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers Using Analog Instrumentation, PDF page 162
notes.evidence: With the exception of the instrument takeoff, all of the maneuvers can be performed on “partial panel,” with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.185(b), what must a pilot do after two-way radio failure in VFR conditions?
notes.back: Continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
notes.explanation: The same applies if VFR conditions are met at any point after the failure.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or if VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, each pilot shall continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After radio failure in IFR conditions, which route comes first in the 91.185(c)(1) list?
notes.back: The route assigned in the last ATC clearance received.
notes.explanation: The later options apply only while being vectored or when no route has been assigned.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)(i)
notes.evidence: By the route assigned in the last ATC clearance received;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Radio fails in IFR conditions while the aircraft is being radar vectored. What route does 91.185 require?
notes.back: Direct from the point of radio failure to the fix, route or airway given in the vector clearance.
notes.explanation: The vector clearance already names where the aircraft was being sent, so that becomes the destination of the direct route.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)(ii)
notes.evidence: If being radar vectored, by the direct route from the point of radio failure to the fix, route, or airway specified in the vector clearance;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After radio failure with no assigned route, which route comes before the filed route?
notes.back: The route ATC has advised may be expected in a further clearance.
notes.explanation: In the list it sits above the filed route and below any assigned route.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)(iii)
notes.evidence: In the absence of an assigned route, by the route that ATC has advised may be expected in a further clearance; or
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After radio failure with no assigned route and no expected route, what route is flown?
notes.back: The route filed in the flight plan.
notes.explanation: It is the last option on the list, used only when nothing more recent exists.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)(iv)
notes.evidence: In the absence of an assigned route or a route that ATC has advised may be expected in a further clearance, by the route filed in the flight plan.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After radio failure in IFR conditions, which of the three candidate altitudes comes from the last clearance?
notes.back: The altitude or flight level assigned in the last ATC clearance received.
notes.explanation: It is only a candidate: the pilot flies the highest of the three for the segment.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(2)(i)
notes.evidence: The altitude or flight level assigned in the last ATC clearance received;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which of the three lost-communications altitudes is set by the terrain and route rather than by ATC?
notes.back: The minimum altitude for IFR operations, converted to a minimum flight level where appropriate.
notes.explanation: Since the highest candidate is flown, the aircraft is never below this minimum.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(2)(ii)
notes.evidence: The minimum altitude (converted, if appropriate, to minimum flight level as prescribed in § 91.121(c)) for IFR operations; or
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which lost-communications altitude comes from what ATC said to expect?
notes.back: The altitude or flight level ATC has advised may be expected in a further clearance.
notes.explanation: It counts only if ATC has actually given it as an expected altitude.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(2)(iii)
notes.evidence: The altitude or flight level ATC has advised may be expected in a further clearance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After radio failure in IFR conditions, the pilot flies the {{c1::highest}} of the three altitudes for the route segment being flown.
notes.back: Highest.
notes.explanation: Because the comparison is made for each route segment, the altitude flown can change from one segment to the next.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(2)
notes.evidence: Altitude. At the highest of the following altitudes or flight levels for the route segment being flown:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides listening on the voice feature of a navigation aid, how should a pilot try to re-establish radio contact?
notes.back: On the previously assigned frequency, or with a flight service station or New York or San Francisco Radio.
notes.explanation: The manual adds that 121.5 MHz is not ruled out and that no method has priority.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 6-4-3 Reestablishing Radio Contact
notes.evidence: In addition to monitoring the NAVAID voice feature, the pilot should attempt to reestablish communications by attempting contact: On the previously assigned frequency; or With an FSS or with New York Radio or San Francisco Radio.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.187(a), which in-flight malfunctions must the pilot in command report to ATC when under IFR in controlled airspace?
notes.back: Malfunctions of navigational, approach or communication equipment, as soon as practical.
notes.explanation: The duty covers any such failure that occurs in flight.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.187 Operation under IFR in controlled airspace: Malfunction reports (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: The pilot in command of each aircraft operated in controlled airspace under IFR shall report as soon as practical to ATC any malfunctions of navigational, approach, or communication equipment occurring in flight.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the first item a 91.187 malfunction report must include?
notes.back: The aircraft identification.
notes.explanation: The report starts by telling ATC which aircraft has the problem.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.187 Operation under IFR in controlled airspace: Malfunction reports (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: the pilot in command shall include the— (1) Aircraft identification;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After identifying the aircraft, which item of a 91.187 report names what has failed?
notes.back: The equipment affected.
notes.explanation: It tells the controller which system is out, before saying how much that matters.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.187 Operation under IFR in controlled airspace: Malfunction reports (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)
notes.evidence: (1) Aircraft identification; (2) Equipment affected;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which 91.187 report item describes how much the failure affects flying IFR in the ATC system?
notes.back: The degree to which the pilot's capability to operate under IFR in the ATC system is impaired.
notes.explanation: This item states the effect of the failure, not just its name.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.187 Operation under IFR in controlled airspace: Malfunction reports (eCFR), paragraph (b)(3)
notes.evidence: Degree to which the capability of the pilot to operate under IFR in the ATC system is impaired; and
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which 91.187 report item tells ATC what help the pilot wants?
notes.back: The nature and extent of assistance desired from ATC.
notes.explanation: It is the last item, turning the report into a request.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.187 Operation under IFR in controlled airspace: Malfunction reports (eCFR), paragraph (b)(4)
notes.evidence: Nature and extent of assistance desired from ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What quick comparison does the Instrument Flying Handbook give for identifying a vacuum failure?
notes.back: Compare the attitude indicator at once with the rate-of-turn indicator and the vertical speed indicator.
notes.explanation: It sets the vacuum-driven attitude indicator against instruments that do not rely on the vacuum.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 11, Analog Instrument Failure, PDF page 332
notes.evidence: comparison of the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Once a failed instrument is identified, what does the handbook say to use to keep control?
notes.back: The remaining functional instruments.
notes.explanation: Control is kept on whatever still works while the failure is dealt with.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 11, Analog Instrument Failure, PDF page 332
notes.evidence: and use the remaining functional instruments to maintain
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In a standard rate turn, how long does a 45 degree heading change take, and at half standard rate?
notes.back: 15 seconds at standard rate; 30 seconds at half standard rate.
notes.explanation: Standard rate is 3 degrees per second, so halving the rate doubles the time.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 7, Timed Turns, PDF page 182
notes.evidence: (3 degrees per second), an airplane turns 45° in 15 seconds; in a half standard rate turn, the airplane turns 45° in 30 seconds.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What sets the magnetic compass apart from the other heading sources in a glass cockpit?
notes.back: It is the only instrument that needs no other source of power to work.
notes.explanation: The handbook names it as the heading source after an AHRS or magnetometer failure.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 7, Compass Turns, PDF page 214
notes.evidence: The magnetic compass is the only instrument that requires
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a failure of the AHRS remove from the primary flight display?
notes.back: All heading and attitude indications.
notes.explanation: The attitude and heading shown on the display come from the AHRS.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 7, Unusual Attitude Recovery with AHRS failure, PDF page 217
notes.evidence: in the loss of all heading and attitude indications on the PFD.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When a flight display fails in a glass cockpit, what mode do the systems revert to?
notes.back: A composite mode, called reversionary.
notes.explanation: It is the display arrangement the system falls back to after a screen failure.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 11, Electronic Flight Display Malfunction, PDF page 329
notes.evidence: a composite mode (called reversionary), which eliminates the
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After the electrical charging system fails, roughly how much battery life does the handbook say remains?
notes.back: Approximately 40 minutes.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives it only as an approximate figure.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 11, Alternator/Generator Failure, PDF page 330
notes.evidence: When a loss of the electrical charging system is experienced, the pilot has approximately 40 minutes of battery life
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After an instrument or system failure, when does the handbook say to declare an emergency, if one is needed?
notes.back: Before the situation deteriorates beyond the pilot's ability to recover.
notes.explanation: In the handbook it usually follows advising ATC of the problem.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 11, Emergency instrumentation, PDF page 332
notes.evidence: if necessary, declare an emergency before the situation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An engine fails in a twin at cruise altitude on instruments. What stays the first priority?
notes.back: Maintaining control of the aeroplane; aircraft have been lost through fixation on the engine problem.
notes.explanation: Cruise speed and height may allow time to diagnose the failure, but control still comes first.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook, chapter 13 Transition to Multiengine Airplanes, Engine Failure During Flight, PDF page 34
notes.evidence: Cruise airspeed allows better airplane control and altitude, which may permit time for a possible diagnosis and remedy of the failure. Maintaining airplane control, however, is still paramount. Airplanes have been lost at altitude due to apparent fixation on the engine problem to the detriment of flying the airplane.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does an approach and landing with one engine inoperative differ from a two-engine one?
notes.back: It is essentially the same, but with less power, asymmetric thrust and a higher-than-normal power setting on the operating engine.
notes.explanation: The handbook flies the pattern at similar altitudes, airspeeds and key positions to a two-engine approach.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook, chapter 13 Transition to Multiengine Airplanes, Engine Inoperative Approach and Landing, PDF page 34
notes.evidence: The traffic pattern should be flown at similar altitudes, airspeeds, and key positions as a two-engine approach. The differences are the reduced power available and the fact that the remaining thrust is asymmetrical. A higher-than-normal power setting is necessary on the operative engine.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does the Airplane Flying Handbook say the pilot should do after engine shutdown and deplaning passengers?
notes.back: A post-flight inspection, including a walk-around to check the general condition of the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls securing the aircraft an essential part of any flight.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook, chapter 2 Ground Operations, Post-Flight, PDF page 23
notes.evidence: A pilot should consider this an essential part of any flight. Securing and Servicing After engine shutdown and deplaning passengers, the pilot should accomplish a post-flight inspection. This includes a walk around to inspect the general condition of the aircraft.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Radio fails in cloud; ten minutes later the aircraft breaks out into VFR conditions 40 miles from the destination. What does 91.185 require?
notes.back: B) Continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
notes.choices:
A) Continue the IFR route and altitude to the destination
B) Continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable
C) Climb back into cloud to follow the clearance
notes.choicesExplained: A: the IFR route and altitude rules apply only when VFR cannot be kept. C: meeting VFR conditions after the failure brings in the VFR rule.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (b) covers VFR conditions met after the failure as well as at the time.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or if VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, each pilot shall continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In cloud, a pilot is being radar vectored toward an airway named in the vector clearance when the radio fails. Which route now?
notes.back: B) Direct from the point of failure to that airway.
notes.choices:
A) Continue on the last heading until reaching a fix
B) Direct from the point of failure to that airway
C) Back to the route filed in the flight plan
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule sends the aircraft direct to the fix, route or airway in the vector clearance. C: the filed route is the last option, used only without an assigned or expected route.
notes.explanation: A vectored aircraft goes direct to what the vector clearance specified.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)(ii)
notes.evidence: If being radar vectored, by the direct route from the point of radio failure to the fix, route, or airway specified in the vector clearance;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Radio fails in IFR conditions. The last assigned altitude is 4,000 feet, the minimum IFR altitude for the segment is 5,000 feet, and no altitude was given to expect. What altitude?
notes.back: C) 5,000 feet.
notes.choices:
A) 4,000 feet
B) 4,500 feet
C) 5,000 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A: the assigned altitude is lower than the minimum IFR altitude here. B: the rule takes the highest value, not a middle one.
notes.explanation: The pilot flies the highest of the candidate altitudes for the segment being flown.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(2)
notes.evidence: Altitude. At the highest of the following altitudes or flight levels for the route segment being flown:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: With a failed radio and no expect-further-clearance time, a pilot reaches the clearance limit, an initial approach fix, 12 minutes before the estimated time of arrival. When should the approach begin?
notes.back: C) As close as possible to the estimated time of arrival.
notes.choices:
A) After holding for 30 minutes
B) Immediately on reaching the fix
C) As close as possible to the estimated time of arrival
notes.choicesExplained: B: arriving early does not change the timing rule. A: the rule ties the start to the estimated time of arrival, not to a set hold.
notes.explanation: Without an expect-further-clearance time, the estimated time of arrival from the filed or amended time en route governs.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(3)(i)
notes.evidence: commence descent or descent and approach as close as possible to the expect-further-clearance time if one has been received, or if one has not been received, as close as possible to the estimated time of arrival as calculated from the filed or amended (with ATC) estimated time en route.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: With a failed radio, a pilot reaches the clearance limit, an en route fix from which no approach begins. No expect-further-clearance time was received. What now?
notes.back: A) Leave on arrival and proceed to a fix from which an approach begins.
notes.choices:
A) Leave on arrival and proceed to a fix from which an approach begins
B) Hold there until the radio is fixed
C) Hold there until the estimated time of arrival
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rule gives a timed exit, not an open-ended hold. C: without an expect-further-clearance time, the limit is left on arrival.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (c)(3)(ii) makes arrival over the limit the time to leave when no such time was given.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.185 IFR operations: Two-way radio communications failure (eCFR), paragraph (c)(3)(ii)
notes.evidence: If the clearance limit is not a fix from which an approach begins, leave the clearance limit at the expect-further-clearance time if one has been received, or if none has been received, upon arrival over the clearance limit, and proceed to a fix from which an approach begins
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot loses two-way radio but the transponder still works. What should the pilot set on it?
notes.back: C) Code 7600.
notes.choices:
A) Keep the assigned code
B) Turn the transponder to standby
C) Code 7600
notes.choicesExplained: A: the manual gives a specific code for radio failure. B: the transponder should keep replying, on the radio-failure code.
notes.explanation: The manual tells the pilot to reply on Mode A/3, Code 7600, while noting radar may not cover the aircraft.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 6-4-2 Transponder Operation During Two-way Communications Failure
notes.evidence: If an aircraft with a coded radar beacon transponder experiences a loss of two-way radio capability, the pilot should adjust the transponder to reply on Mode A/3, Code 7600.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Approach control stops answering. The pilot has a second radio and can reach a flight service station. What does the manual advise?
notes.back: A) Try the previously assigned frequency and the flight service station, together if possible.
notes.choices:
A) Try the previously assigned frequency and the flight service station, together if possible
B) Use only 121.5 MHz
C) Stay silent until the next clearance limit
notes.choicesExplained: B: 121.5 MHz is allowed, but it is not the only option. C: the manual expects active attempts to re-establish contact.
notes.explanation: Both routes back to ATC are listed, and the manual says there is no priority between them.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 6-4-3 Reestablishing Radio Contact
notes.evidence: In addition to monitoring the NAVAID voice feature, the pilot should attempt to reestablish communications by attempting contact: On the previously assigned frequency; or With an FSS or with New York Radio or San Francisco Radio.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After radio failure, following 91.185 exactly would take a pilot with a sick passenger to a distant destination. Who decides whether this is an emergency?
notes.back: C) The pilot, who may deviate as far as the emergency requires.
notes.choices:
A) No one: radio failure is never an emergency
B) ATC, once contact is regained
C) The pilot, who may deviate as far as the emergency requires
notes.choicesExplained: A: whether it is an emergency depends on the circumstances. B: the manual makes it the pilot's determination.
notes.explanation: The manual leaves the call to the pilot and points to the emergency authority in 91.3(b).
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 6-4-1 Two-way Radio Communications Failure
notes.evidence: Whether two-way communications failure constitutes an emergency depends on the circumstances, and in any event, it is a determination made by the pilot. 14 CFR section 91.3(b) authorizes a pilot to deviate from any rule in Subparts A and B to the extent required to meet an emergency.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under IFR in controlled airspace, the glide slope receiver fails in flight. What must the pilot in command do?
notes.back: B) Report it to ATC as soon as practical.
notes.choices:
A) Report it only after landing
B) Report it to ATC as soon as practical
C) Report it only if an ILS approach is planned
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule requires a report in flight, as soon as practical. C: the duty covers any approach equipment malfunction, whatever the plan.
notes.explanation: Approach equipment failures in flight must be reported to ATC as soon as practical.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.187 Operation under IFR in controlled airspace: Malfunction reports (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: The pilot in command of each aircraft operated in controlled airspace under IFR shall report as soon as practical to ATC any malfunctions of navigational, approach, or communication equipment occurring in flight.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In cloud, the attitude indicator shows a slow roll to the left, while the turn coordinator shows wings level and the vertical speed indicator is steady. What is most likely?
notes.back: C) The attitude indicator is failing.
notes.choices:
A) The aircraft is really turning left
B) The turn coordinator has failed
C) The attitude indicator is failing
notes.choicesExplained: B: the turn coordinator agrees with the steady vertical speed indicator. A: a real turn would show on the turn coordinator.
notes.explanation: Comparing the attitude indicator with the turn and vertical speed instruments exposes the odd one out.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 11, Analog Instrument Failure, PDF page 332
notes.evidence: comparison of the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: With the heading indicator failed, a pilot needs a 90 degree heading change at standard rate. How long should the turn last?
notes.back: A) 30 seconds.
notes.choices:
A) 30 seconds
B) 15 seconds
C) 45 seconds
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the time for 45 degrees. C: that would give 135 degrees at 3 degrees per second.
notes.explanation: At 3 degrees per second, 45 degrees takes 15 seconds, so 90 degrees takes 30.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 7, Timed Turns, PDF page 182
notes.evidence: (3 degrees per second), an airplane turns 45° in 15 seconds; in a half standard rate turn, the airplane turns 45° in 30 seconds.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The AHRS fails in cloud and the display loses its heading. What does the handbook say the pilot uses to determine heading?
notes.back: B) The magnetic compass.
notes.choices:
A) The heading on the primary flight display
B) The magnetic compass
C) The turn coordinator alone
notes.choicesExplained: A: the display's heading comes from the failed AHRS. C: the turn coordinator shows rate of turn, not heading.
notes.explanation: The handbook names the magnetic compass for heading after an AHRS or magnetometer failure.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 7, Compass Turns, PDF page 214
notes.evidence: AHRS or magnetometer failure, the magnetic compass is
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In a glass cockpit, the primary flight display screen goes blank. What should the pilot expect from the system?
notes.back: C) A composite reversionary mode on the remaining display.
notes.choices:
A) The engine display alone
B) All flight information lost until landing
C) A composite reversionary mode on the remaining display
notes.choicesExplained: B: the system is designed to revert, not to lose everything. A: reversionary mode combines information rather than keeping one page.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the systems revert to a composite mode called reversionary.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 11, Electronic Flight Display Malfunction, PDF page 329
notes.evidence: a composite mode (called reversionary), which eliminates the
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Twenty minutes after takeoff in cloud, the alternator fails and cannot be reset. The destination is an hour away; a suitable airport is 15 minutes away. What does the handbook advise?
notes.back: B) Land at the nearest suitable airport.
notes.choices:
A) Continue, and decide once the battery runs low
B) Land at the nearest suitable airport
C) Continue to the destination on the battery
notes.choicesExplained: A: waiting for a low battery is the same continuation it rules out. C: the handbook says never to consider continuing once charging has failed.
notes.explanation: With the charging system gone, the handbook points to the nearest suitable airport.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), chapter 11, Alternator/Generator Failure, PDF page 330
notes.evidence: system has failed. Land at the nearest suitable airport.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force
